key_insight: The paper shows that visual navigation becomes safer and more efficient when the robot learns an adaptive safety margin instead of relying on a fixed one. A context-conditioned safety critic selects among candidate trajectories by estimating how much clearance is needed in each scene.
problem_solved: It addresses the mismatch between fixed safety margins and real indoor environments. Too-conservative margins cause unnecessary detours and failures, while too-permissive margins increase collision risk, especially when perception is biased or uncertain.
method: Use a diffusion-based planner to generate diverse candidate trajectories from egocentric RGB-D input.
Train a context-conditioned safety critic to predict an adaptive clearance preference for the current scene.
Select the trajectory that best balances safety and efficiency rather than using a one-size-fits-all margin.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a practical way to improve navigation reliability without redesigning the planner itself. It can reduce failed runs, shorten paths, and make robot behavior more robust in cluttered indoor spaces.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram: RGB-D input -> diffusion planner -> safety critic -> selected path.
A side-by-side comparison of fixed margin vs adaptive margin navigation in a cluttered room.
A risk-versus-efficiency chart showing conservative, balanced, and permissive behavior.
Icons for obstacles, clearance buffer, and trajectory candidates to illustrate decision-making.
paper_title: Learning Adaptive Safety Margins for Visual Navigation
paper_authors: Junyi Hu, Shuaihang Yuan, Geeta Chandra Raju Bethala, Anthony Tzes, Yi Fang
